regions.name: Tejo
regions.summary: The Tejo is the wine country of the Tagus, the river that reaches the sea at Lisbon, and until 2009 it was called the Ribatejo. It is a region of value: warm, fertile and flat along the river, sandier and hotter on the south bank, hillier and cooler on the north. Fernão Pires leads the whites, Castelão and Trincadeira the traditional reds, and Touriga Nacional, Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon the modern ones. Most of what is poured carries the Vinho Regional Tejo label rather than the DOC, because the regional tier has the longer grape list and the looser rules. For the exam, hold the three zones, the lead grapes and the old name.

terroir.climate: Warm and dry in summer with a Mediterranean pattern of winter rain, but the Tagus estuary lets Atlantic air up the valley, so the river plain is milder and more humid than the plains to the east. The south bank is the hottest and driest ground; the northern hills towards Tomar are cooler and wetter. Frost is rare and ripeness is seldom the problem; keeping acidity is.
terroir.soils: Three soils, one per zone: deep alluvial silt and clay on the floodplain, fertile enough to make vines vigorous; poor sand with some gravel on the south bank, the Charneca; and clay with limestone, some schist and sandstone in the northern hills, the Bairro. The hills and the sand give the better wines, the plain the bigger yields.
terroir.topography: A broad, low river valley running south-west towards Lisbon. The Lezíria, the floodplain of the Tagus, is almost flat and floods in a wet winter. North of the river the land rises into rolling hills and small ridges; south of it the Charneca is a low, dry plain of sand, pine and cork oak.
terroir.water: The Tejo, the Tagus, is the whole point: it floods the Campo, carries sea air inland and divides the clay north bank from the sandy south bank. The Zêzere, which joins it from the north, and the Nabão, which runs through Tomar, cut the northern hills.

grapes.name: Fernão Pires
grapes.styles: The region's white workhorse, aromatic and soft, grapey and floral, best drunk young and often blended with Arinto for acidity; Bairrada calls the same grape Maria Gomes.

grapes.name: Castelão
grapes.styles: The red of the sandy south bank, medium-bodied, raspberry and dried herb, firm when young and leathery with age; the grape sold for decades as Periquita.

grapes.name: Trincadeira
grapes.styles: Spicy, peppery and dark fruited when it ripens cleanly, and prone to rot in a damp autumn; the lift in many traditional blends. It is Tinta Amarela in the north.

grapes.name: Touriga Nacional
grapes.styles: Planted widely since the 1990s for perfume, colour and structure in the ambitious reds of the Bairro and the Charneca.

grapes.name: Arinto
grapes.styles: The acid-keeping white blended with Fernão Pires; on its own it is lean, lemony and able to take a little oak.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: The international red that has taken best to the Tejo's heat, giving ripe, dark, peppery wines under the Vinho Regional label.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Grown for blends with Touriga Nacional and for varietal bottlings; it ripens fully in the Charneca's sand.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.styles: As Tinta Roriz or Aragonez, a filler of colour and body in reds that lead with Touriga or Castelão.

wines.note: Fernão Pires with Arinto, sometimes Sauvignon Blanc or Chardonnay: aromatic, soft, orange blossom and pear, drunk cold and young with grilled fish, clams and salads. The glass pour of the region.

A blend led by Castelão, Trincadeira and Touriga Nacional from the Bairro or the Charneca: medium to full, ripe red and black fruit, dried herb, moderate tannin, a year or two of oak in the Reserva. It takes roast pork, duck and grilled lamb.
Where most of the Syrah and the international blends go: ripe, plush, generous reds at a kind price, the Tejo's calling card abroad. Serve a touch cool with burgers, barbecue and spiced dishes.
Castelão or Touriga Nacional pressed pink: strawberry, dry and light, a summer wine for the river towns and for charcuterie.
A small production of traditional method sparkling, often Fernão Pires and Arinto, crisp and simple, poured as an aperitif.

made.viticulture: The Tejo was planted for volume: the Lezíria's deep silt makes vines grow like weeds, and through the twentieth century the floodplain and its co-operatives filled bulk wine for Lisbon and the colonies. Since the 1990s the better growers have moved the vine off the plain, where the state has paid to pull vineyards and plant other crops, and onto the clay-limestone hills of the Bairro and the sand of the Charneca, which stress the vine, cut the yield and ripen a smaller, darker grape. Training is on wires with spur or cane pruning, rows wide enough for machines on the flat and tighter on the slopes. Irrigation is allowed and common on the sand, where the summer is dry and the soil holds nothing. Harvest runs from mid August for the whites into late September for Touriga and Cabernet, by machine on the big estates and by hand on the old mixed plots. The hazards are rot in Trincadeira after an autumn rain, sunburn on the south bank and the loss of acidity in a hot year, which is why Arinto stays in every white blend. The fruit shares the land with horses, fighting bulls, cork oak, olives and rice: the Ribatejo was always a farm before it was a vineyard.
made.winemaking: The whites are made cold and fast: night picking or early morning, gentle pressing, settling, a cool fermentation in stainless steel and bottling within months, so that Fernão Pires keeps the floral lift that it loses with age. A few estates ferment Arinto or Chardonnay in barrel and leave it on the lees for weight. The reds are destemmed, fermented in steel or in concrete at moderate temperatures with pumping over, and the serious ones go to French or American oak for a year, with Reserva and Garrafeira carrying the national rules on alcohol and time. The Tejo's style is ripe and rounded rather than tannic, and winemakers blend for it: Touriga Nacional for perfume and colour, Castelão for freshness and tannin, Trincadeira for spice, Syrah or Cabernet for flesh. The regional tier, Vinho Regional Tejo, carries the longer grape list and the looser rules, which is why most labels wear it; the DOC's lists are narrower and drawn sub-region by sub-region, though they admit Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot beside the Portuguese grapes. Traditional method sparkling and a little sweet or late harvest wine are made but seldom leave the region.

law.classification: The DOC Ribatejo took its statute by decree in 2000, with the regional wine around it as Vinho Regional Ribatejano. In 2009 both were renamed after the river, DOC do Tejo and Vinho Regional Tejo, so that the labels and the region's name agreed and the old name's association with bulk wine was shed. The DOC carries six sub-regions that may be named on the label: Almeirim, Cartaxo, Chamusca, Coruche, Santarém and Tomar. The DOC's grape lists are drawn sub-region by sub-region and rest on Fernão Pires, Arinto, Castelão, Trincadeira and Touriga Nacional, with Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot admitted in the statute of 2000; the Vinho Regional, under the Comissão Vitivinícola Regional do Tejo, carries a longer list still, Syrah, Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc among them, and looser rules. The three zones, Bairro, Campo and Charneca, are the growers' and the trade's words for the terroir, not legal names on a label. Reserva and Garrafeira follow the national rules.
tiers: DOC do Tejo
The appellation of the Tagus valley, called DOC Ribatejo until 2009: its own grape lists, drawn sub-region by sub-region, and six sub-regions that may be named.
DOC do Tejo with a sub-region
Almeirim, Cartaxo, Chamusca, Coruche, Santarém or Tomar on the label: the wine comes from that sub-region alone.
Vinho Regional Tejo
The regional wine, formerly Ribatejano, over the same land: a longer grape list, looser rules, and the tier most Tejo wine wears.
Vinho
Wine with no origin claim, the old vinho de mesa; the floodplain's bulk wine lived here.
labels: Ribatejo
The region's name until 2009; it means the banks of the Tagus and still appears on older bottles.
Bairro
The northern hills of clay and limestone, the zone of the firmer reds.
Charneca
The sandy, dry south bank, warm and poor, where Castelão and the international reds ripen.
Campo or Lezíria
The alluvial floodplain of the river, fertile and high yielding.
Reserva
A vintage-dated wine of at least half a degree more alcohol than the regional minimum, often oaked.
Colheita Seleccionada
A selected harvest, vintage dated, held to its own alcohol floor above the regional minimum.
Quinta, Casal, Herdade
Estate names; the Tejo's great farms are quintas and casais.

places.name: Bairro
places.note: The north bank's hills of clay, limestone and some schist, running from Santarém up to Tomar: cooler, wetter and later than the plain, the source of the Tejo's most structured reds and of its firmest Arinto.

places.name: Tomar
places.note: The northernmost sub-region, around the Templar town on the Nabão: the coolest and hilliest corner of the Tejo, with limestone and schist and fresher whites.

places.name: Santarém
places.note: The regional capital above the river, with the Bairro's slopes behind it; its name is one of the six sub-regions of the DOC.

places.name: Cartaxo
places.note: A sub-region on the north bank below Santarém, part hill and part plain, long a centre of co-operative production and now of estate reds.

places.name: Campo
places.note: The Lezíria, the floodplain of the Tagus: deep, fertile silt that floods in winter and gives huge crops of soft wine. It carried the region's bulk trade and is now largely given to other crops, with vines kept where the levees hold the soil drier.

places.name: Almeirim
places.note: The sub-region on the south bank opposite Santarém, where the plain meets the sand and the Tejo's oldest estates stand; the fullest reds of the DOC come from its edge.

places.name: Chamusca
places.note: A riverside sub-region upstream of Almeirim on the plain, with cork oak and rice beside the vines.

places.name: Charneca
places.note: The south bank's dry plain of sand, pine, cork oak and heath: poor, hot and well drained, it ripens Castelão, Syrah and Cabernet to a dark, soft wine. Irrigation is usual here.

places.name: Coruche
places.note: The southernmost sub-region, on the Sorraia river in the sand of the Charneca, next to the cork oak country of the Alentejo.

producers.name: Quinta da Alorna
producers.why: An Almeirim estate dating from 1723, named for a marquisate won in India, and one of the Tejo's oldest names for estate reds and Fernão Pires.

producers.name: Casal Branco
producers.why: An old family estate at Almeirim whose falconry label carries the Tejo's firmer traditional-grape reds and oak-aged whites.

producers.name: Quinta da Lagoalva de Cima
producers.why: A large estate at Alpiarça on the south bank that grows Touriga Nacional and Syrah beside horses and cork, the modern Tejo on one farm.

producers.name: Companhia das Lezírias
producers.why: The great farm company of the floodplain, founded in 1836, which shows what the Campo and the Charneca sand can do when yields are held down.

exam: Place the Tejo on the Tagus north-east of Lisbon, inland from Lisboa and north of the Alentejo, and know it was the Ribatejo until 2009.
Name the three zones, Bairro, Campo and Charneca, and say which is clay hills, which floodplain and which sand.
Give the lead grapes: Fernão Pires and Arinto for white, Castelão, Trincadeira and Touriga Nacional for red.
Know that most Tejo wine is sold as Vinho Regional Tejo, the tier with the longer grape list and the looser rules.
Hold the synonyms: Fernão Pires is Maria Gomes in Bairrada, Castelão was sold as Periquita, Trincadeira is Tinta Amarela.
traps: The Tejo is a river region and a wine region; Lisboa is the coastal region beside it, and both were renamed in the same years (Lisboa was Estremadura).
Bairro is a zone of the Tejo; Bairrada is a separate DOC far to the north on clay by the Atlantic.
The Tejo's sand is the Charneca on the south bank; the clay is on the north bank, the opposite of what a reader guesses from the Alentejo.
Tinta Roriz and Aragonez are both Tempranillo, and the Tejo uses both names.
Vinho Regional Tejo is not a lesser wine in quality terms: the estates choose it for its freedom in grapes and blending.

cards.b: Ribatejo, the banks of the Tagus; the DOC and the Vinho Regional were both renamed Tejo in 2009.

cards.f: Three zones of the Tejo and their soils
cards.b: Bairro, clay and limestone hills on the north bank; Campo or Lezíria, the alluvial floodplain; Charneca, the sandy, dry south bank.

cards.f: Lead white grape of the Tejo
cards.b: Fernão Pires, aromatic and soft, usually blended with Arinto for acidity; it is Maria Gomes in Bairrada.

cards.f: Traditional red grapes of the Tejo
cards.b: Castelão and Trincadeira, with Touriga Nacional since the 1990s; Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon go mostly into the Vinho Regional blends.

cards.f: Why most Tejo wine is Vinho Regional
cards.b: The regional tier carries the longer grape list (Syrah, Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc among them) and the looser rules; the DOC's lists are narrower and drawn sub-region by sub-region.

cards.f: Six sub-regions of DOC do Tejo
cards.b: Almeirim, Cartaxo, Chamusca, Coruche, Santarém and Tomar.

cards.f: Which Tejo zone is the sandy one?
cards.b: The Charneca, on the south bank: hot, poor and well drained, home to Castelão and the ripe international reds.

questions.q: Under which name was the Tejo wine region known until 2009?
questions.exp: Ribatejo, the banks of the Tagus, became Tejo in 2009. Estremadura became Lisboa and Terras do Sado became Península de Setúbal in the same wave of renaming; Beira Interior kept its name.

questions.q: What is the English name of the river that gives the Tejo region its name?
questions.exp: The Tejo is the Portuguese name of the Tagus, which rises in Spain as the Tajo and meets the Atlantic at Lisbon; the Bairro hills lie north of it and the Charneca sand south.

questions.q: Which zone of the Tejo is the sandy, dry plain of the south bank?
questions.exp: The Charneca is the poor sand and heath south of the river, warm and well drained. The Bairro is the clay and limestone hills north of it, and Campo and Lezíria are two names for the alluvial floodplain.

questions.q: Which white grape leads the blends of the Tejo?
questions.exp: Fernão Pires, aromatic and soft, is the Tejo's and Lisboa's white workhorse, usually with Arinto for acidity. Encruzado belongs to the Dão, Alvarinho to Vinho Verde and Antão Vaz to the Alentejo.

questions.q: Under which name is Fernão Pires grown in Bairrada?
questions.exp: The same aromatic white carries two names: Fernão Pires in the Tejo, Lisboa and the south, Maria Gomes in Bairrada, where it goes into the sparkling wine.

questions.q: Which red grape of the Tejo is known as Tinta Amarela in the Douro?
questions.exp: Trincadeira, spicy and peppery when it ripens cleanly but prone to rot in a damp autumn, is Tinta Amarela in the Douro, where it goes into Port. Castelão is the Charneca's red, long sold as Periquita; Baga belongs to Bairrada and Alfrocheiro to the Dão.

questions.q: Why do most Tejo wines carry the Vinho Regional Tejo label rather than the DOC?
opts: The regional tier has a longer grape list and looser rules
The DOC rules permit only white and rosé wine to carry the Tejo name
The regional tier requires two years of ageing in new oak barrels
The DOC applies only to sparkling and sweet wines of the valley
questions.exp: The DOC's grape lists are narrower and drawn sub-region by sub-region, while Vinho Regional Tejo carries a longer list, Syrah and Chardonnay among them, and looser rules, which suits the estates' export blends; the DOC covers still wine of every colour.

regions.name: Setúbal
regions.summary: The Setúbal peninsula lies across the Tagus from Lisbon, between that estuary and the Sado's, with the limestone ridge of the Arrábida along its southern shore and warm sand inland. It gives the exam two things: Moscatel de Setúbal, a fortified Muscat of Alexandria macerated on its skins after fortification and aged in wood for years and sometimes for decades, and Palmela, the DOC of Castelão reds on sand. Around both sits Vinho Regional Península de Setúbal, called Terras do Sado until 2009, where Syrah, Cabernet and Touriga Nacional make the peninsula's modern reds. One family house has defined the region since 1834.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean with the Atlantic close: warm, dry summers and mild, wet winters, the sea breeze crossing the peninsula every afternoon. The Arrábida's south-facing slopes above the water are the warmest and ripen Moscatel to high sugar; the sandy plain of Palmela is hot by day and cool at night; the northern shore facing the Tagus is the coolest ground.
terroir.soils: Two soils, one wine each. The Serra da Arrábida is limestone and clay, pale and stony, and it gives the Moscatel its ripeness and its grip. The Palmela plain is deep, poor sand over clay, warm and free draining, where Castelão roots deep and ripens evenly; phylloxera travels badly through it, so some old vines remain on their own roots.
terroir.topography: A broad peninsula pointing south-west, flat and low across most of its width, with the Arrábida rising abruptly to about five hundred metres along the south coast and dropping to the sea in cliffs. The best Moscatel grows on its north and south flanks around Azeitão; the Castelão country is the sandy plain north and east of Palmela's castle hill.
terroir.water: The Tagus to the north and the Sado to the south are both estuaries, and between them the peninsula is never far from salt water. The Sado gave the old regional name, Terras do Sado, and its mouth at Setúbal is the port the Moscatel sailed from.

grapes.name: Moscatel de Setúbal
grapes.styles: Muscat of Alexandria under its local name: big-berried, high in sugar, grapey and orange-scented, grown on the Arrábida's limestone for the fortified wine that carries the region's name.

grapes.name: Moscatel Roxo
grapes.styles: A pink-skinned Muscat, rare and prized, which makes a more perfumed, rose-tinged fortified wine labelled Moscatel Roxo de Setúbal.

grapes.name: Castelão
grapes.styles: The peninsula's red, at home on Palmela's sand: raspberry, dried herb and tobacco, firm in youth and gentle after a decade; the grape behind the Periquita brand since 1850.

grapes.name: Fernão Pires
grapes.styles: The aromatic white of the plain, soft and floral, drunk young or blended with Arinto in the regional whites.

grapes.name: Arinto
grapes.styles: The acid in the white blends, lemony and firm, and the grape of the few serious dry whites of the peninsula.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Ripe, dark and peppery on the sand, a mainstay of the regional reds and of many Castelão blends.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Planted in the Arrábida foothills from the 1970s for a Bordeaux-styled estate red that put the peninsula's table wine on the map.

grapes.name: Touriga Nacional
grapes.styles: Perfume and colour in the regional blends, usually beside Castelão and Syrah.

wines.note: Amber to gold, around seventeen to eighteen per cent, sweet and grapey when young with orange peel and honey, darkening to toffee, dried fig and bitter marmalade with decades in wood; the acidity keeps it lively. Serve cool in a small glass with almond tart, orange desserts, crème caramel or blue cheese, or on its own after dinner.
The rare pink Muscat: rosier, spicier and more floral than the white, usually released older and poured as a rarity by the glass.

Castelão-led red from the sand, raspberry and tobacco, medium-bodied with a firm, dry finish, softened by a year in oak in the Reserva; the classic pairing is roast kid, grilled sardines or a plate of cured ham.

wines.style: Vinho Regional Península de Setúbal tinto
wines.note: Blends of Castelão, Syrah, Touriga Nacional, Aragonez and Cabernet: ripe, dark, easy reds at a kind price, served slightly cool with grilled meats.
Fernão Pires and Arinto, sometimes Chardonnay or Verdelho: soft, aromatic, cold, for the fried fish and shellfish of the Sado coast.

made.viticulture: The Moscatel grows where the Arrábida's limestone gives way to clay around Azeitão, on low vines in rows; Muscat of Alexandria needs the heat of that south-facing wall of rock to reach the sugar the fortified wine wants, and it is picked late, in September, at high ripeness. Moscatel Roxo is planted in small, treasured parcels. On the Palmela plain Castelão is grown on sand, bush trained in the old vineyards and on wire in the new, the roots going deep for water; the sand drains so fast that vigour is low and the grape ripens small and even, and because phylloxera moves poorly through pure sand some old plots stand on their own roots. Irrigation is allowed and used on the plain. The hazards are different in the two zones: on the Arrábida, drought and the sea wind; on the sand, heat spikes that cook the fruit and the autumn humidity off the two estuaries that brings rot to thin-skinned grapes. Harvest begins in August for the whites and the Syrah and runs to late September for Castelão and the Moscatel. The international reds planted since the 1970s, Cabernet first and Syrah after, sit in the foothills and on the plain's edge.
made.winemaking: Moscatel de Setúbal is made the way the French make a vin doux naturel, with one step of its own. The must ferments on its skins for a few days, then grape spirit is added before the sugar is gone, stopping the yeast and leaving the wine sweet at around seventeen to eighteen per cent alcohol. The skins are then returned, or left, in the fortified wine for months through the winter, and that maceration after fortification is what gives the wine its deep orange-peel aroma and its grip; few other Muscats are made this way. The wine is racked off the skins in spring and goes to old wood, where it ages oxidatively: a few years for the basic bottling, five, ten, twenty, thirty or forty years for the aged wines sold with an age indication, and a lifetime for the oldest casks that the lodges still hold. A Colheita is one harvest; Superior marks a selected lot. The red table wines of Palmela are made in the modern Portuguese way, destemmed, fermented in stainless steel or concrete, aged in French and American oak for the Reserva; Castelão takes well to old wood and to a few years in bottle. The regional whites are cold fermented and bottled young.

law.classification: The peninsula holds two DOCs and a regional wine. DOC Setúbal is the fortified Muscat: a wine labelled Moscatel de Setúbal or Moscatel Roxo de Setúbal must take at least 85 per cent of its must from that grape, and a wine with at least 67 per cent Moscatel may be labelled plainly Setúbal, under the statute of the denomination. The DOC admits age indications on the aged blends and the terms Colheita and Superior. DOC Palmela, demarcated on the sandy plain, is for table wine and requires its reds to be at least two thirds Castelão; whites and rosés are also allowed. Vinho Regional Península de Setúbal covers the whole peninsula with a wider grape list, and it was called Terras do Sado until the renaming of 2009. The Comissão Vitivinícola Regional da Península de Setúbal certifies all three.
tiers: DOC Setúbal
The fortified Muscat: Moscatel de Setúbal or Moscatel Roxo de Setúbal needs at least 85 per cent of that grape; plain Setúbal at least 67 per cent.
DOC Palmela
Table wine from the sandy plain; a red must be at least two thirds Castelão.
Vinho Regional Península de Setúbal
The regional wine over the whole peninsula, Terras do Sado until 2009; it takes Syrah, Cabernet, Touriga Nacional and the rest.
Vinho
Wine with no origin claim.
labels: Moscatel de Setúbal
Fortified Muscat of Alexandria from the DOC, at least 85 per cent of the grape.
Moscatel Roxo
The pink-skinned Muscat, labelled Moscatel Roxo de Setúbal.
Setúbal
On its own: the fortified wine with 67 to 85 per cent Moscatel.
Superior
A selected lot of Moscatel of higher quality, held longer before release.
10 Anos, 20 Anos, 30 Anos, 40 Anos
An age indication on an aged Moscatel blend; the number describes the blend, not one harvest.
Colheita
A Moscatel from a single harvest, vintage dated.
Periquita
A brand name of the oldest house that became a popular synonym for Castelão; the grape's name on a label is Castelão.
Terras do Sado
The regional wine's name until 2009, still on older bottles.

places.name: Serra da Arrábida
places.note: The limestone ridge along the south coast, rising to about five hundred metres and falling to the sea in cliffs: its clay and limestone flanks grow the Moscatel de Setúbal and the peninsula's Cabernet, and its slopes are a natural park, so the vineyards stop at the trees.

places.name: Azeitão
places.note: The village at the foot of the Arrábida where the region's two historic houses have their lodges and cellars: the home of Moscatel de Setúbal, of the Periquita brand and of the peninsula's first Cabernet, with a sheep's cheese and a sweet pastry of its own.

places.name: Palmela
places.note: The castle town and the DOC of the sandy plain north and east of it: Castelão on deep, poor sand, some of it ungrafted, making the firm raspberry-and-tobacco reds that soften over ten years. The co-operative at Pegões and the family estates of Fernando Pó are its working heart.

places.name: Pegões
places.note: The village on the plain whose co-operative, founded in the 1950s on a government settlement scheme, became the peninsula's most reliable source of inexpensive Castelão, Syrah and Fernão Pires.

places.name: Setúbal
places.note: The port city on the Sado estuary, a harbour of fishing and shipping, which gave the fortified wine its name and shipped it; the vineyards lie west of it under the Arrábida.

places.name: Sado estuary
places.note: The river mouth south of the peninsula, salt marsh, rice and dolphins, which named the regional wine until 2009 and sends the morning humidity over the Palmela sand.

producers.name: José Maria da Fonseca
producers.why: The Azeitão house founded in 1834 that made Moscatel de Setúbal a category, created Periquita in 1850 and holds the oldest casks on the peninsula; it is not the Port house.

producers.name: Bacalhôa Vinhos de Portugal
producers.why: The Azeitão company, formerly J.P. Vinhos, whose Quinta da Bacalhôa Cabernet of the 1970s and aged Moscatels made it the region's other reference.

producers.name: Adega de Pegões
producers.why: The co-operative of the Palmela plain, the dependable source of the peninsula's everyday Castelão, Syrah and Fernão Pires at every price.

producers.name: Casa Ermelinda Freitas
producers.why: A family estate at Fernando Pó on the Palmela sand that built its name on Castelão and old-vine reds under the DOC Palmela and the regional label.

exam: Place the peninsula south of Lisbon between the Tagus and Sado estuaries, with the Arrábida on its south coast and the Palmela sand inland.
Define Moscatel de Setúbal: Muscat of Alexandria, fortified during fermentation, macerated on its skins after fortification, aged oxidatively in wood.
Know the two DOCs and the regional wine: Setúbal for the fortified Muscat, Palmela for Castelão table wine, Península de Setúbal (Terras do Sado until 2009) around them.
Give Castelão as the red grape of the sand and Periquita as the brand name that became its nickname.
Separate the two Fonsecas: José Maria da Fonseca of Azeitão and Fonseca the Port shipper of Gaia.
At the Advanced level hold the percentages, 85 for the traditional names and 67 for plain Setúbal, and Moscatel Roxo.
traps: Moscatel de Setúbal is Muscat of Alexandria, the big-berried Muscat; the Douro's Moscatel Galego, Beaumes-de-Venise and Frontignan are the small-berried Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains.
Setúbal DOC is a fortified wine only; the peninsula's table wines are Palmela DOC or Vinho Regional Península de Setúbal.
Periquita is a brand, not a grape: the grape is Castelão, and the brand belongs to one house.
José Maria da Fonseca is a Setúbal table and Moscatel house; Fonseca is a Port house. Two different families, two different wines.
The skins are returned after fortification, not before; that is what sets this Muscat apart from a vin doux naturel.
An age indication on a Moscatel (10, 20, 30, 40 Anos) describes a blend; Colheita names one harvest.
Terras do Sado on an older label is the same regional wine as Península de Setúbal.

cards.b: Muscat of Alexandria, the big-berried Muscat, under its local name; Moscatel Roxo is its rare pink-skinned relative.

cards.f: The step that sets Moscatel de Setúbal apart from a vin doux naturel
cards.b: After fortification the skins go back into the wine for months, through the winter, for a deep orange-peel aroma and grip.

cards.f: The two DOCs of the Setúbal peninsula
cards.b: Setúbal, the fortified Muscat; Palmela, Castelão table wine on sand. Around them, Vinho Regional Península de Setúbal.

cards.f: Minimum Castelão in a red Palmela DOC
cards.b: Two thirds, 67 per cent; Castelão is the grape sold for generations as Periquita.
Terras do Sado, after the estuary on the peninsula's south side.

cards.f: Moscatel percentage for the name Moscatel de Setúbal
cards.b: At least 85 per cent of the must from the grape; a wine with 67 to 85 per cent is labelled plainly Setúbal.
José Maria da Fonseca, Azeitão, founded 1834: Moscatel de Setúbal and Periquita. Fonseca of Vila Nova de Gaia: Port.
Cool, in a small glass, with almond or orange desserts, crème caramel or blue cheese; an opened bottle keeps for weeks.

questions.q: Which grape variety is Moscatel de Setúbal?
questions.exp: Moscatel de Setúbal is the local name of Muscat of Alexandria, the large-berried Muscat of hot climates. The small-berried Muscat Blanc makes Beaumes-de-Venise and Asti, Ottonel is Alsace's and Moscato Giallo is Alpine Italy's.

questions.q: What happens to the grape skins in the making of Moscatel de Setúbal after the wine has been fortified?
opts: They go back into the wine and macerate for months
They are pressed again to make a second, drier wine
They are distilled into the fortifying spirit
They are dried for a passito-style sweetening
questions.exp: The maceration after fortification, through the winter, is the step that marks the wine: it gives the orange-peel intensity and grip that a vin doux naturel, racked off its skins at fortification, does not have.

questions.q: Which DOC of the Setúbal peninsula covers its Castelão-led table reds grown on sand?
questions.exp: Palmela is the DOC of the sandy plain north and east of the castle town, and its reds must be at least two thirds Castelão; the Setúbal DOC is for the fortified Muscat only.

questions.q: Which red grape makes the wine sold for generations under the brand name Periquita?
questions.exp: Castelão is the red of sandy southern Portugal, and Periquita is a brand of the oldest Setúbal house that became its nickname. Trincadeira is the spicy Alentejo partner, Aragonez is Tempranillo and Touriga Franca is the Douro's Port workhorse.

questions.q: What was the Vinho Regional Península de Setúbal called before 2009?
questions.exp: The regional wine took its old name from the Sado estuary on the peninsula's south side and was renamed in 2009, as Ribatejo became Tejo; Estremadura became Lisboa in the same years.

questions.q: Which limestone ridge along the peninsula's south coast grows the best Moscatel de Setúbal?
questions.exp: The Arrábida rises to about five hundred metres above the sea west of Setúbal, and its clay and limestone flanks around Azeitão ripen the Muscat. Sintra stands over the sand of Colares, the Estrela shelters the Dão and São Mamede is the Alentejo's Portalegre.

questions.q: Which house of Azeitão is the reference for Moscatel de Setúbal and created the Periquita brand?
questions.exp: José Maria da Fonseca, founded in 1834, is the Setúbal house of Moscatel and Periquita; Bacalhôa is Azeitão's other house, known for Cabernet and aged Moscatel; Fonseca Guimaraens is the Port shipper of Gaia and Quinta do Noval a Port house of the Douro.

questions.q: What is the minimum share of the named grape in a wine labelled Moscatel de Setúbal?
questions.exp: The traditional names Moscatel de Setúbal and Moscatel Roxo de Setúbal need at least 85 per cent of the must from that grape; a wine with at least 67 per cent may be labelled plainly Setúbal, and 75 and 100 are not thresholds in this DOC.

regions.name: Alentejo
regions.summary: The Alentejo is the land beyond the Tagus, a third of Portugal of rolling plain, cork oak, olive and wheat, hot and dry through a long summer. Its reds are ripe, soft and generous, blends of Aragonez, Trincadeira, Alicante Bouschet and Castelão with Syrah and Touriga Nacional beside them, and its whites lean on Antão Vaz with Arinto for acidity. The DOC Alentejo has eight sub-regions, Portalegre on granite at altitude the cool exception, and the regional wine Alentejano covers the rest. Two traditions stand out: wine fermented in clay talhas, and the cork forests that stopper the world's bottles.

terroir.climate: Hot, dry and continental, among the hottest and driest ground on the mainland: summers above forty degrees are common, rainfall is low and falls in winter, and the south-east around Moura and Granja-Amareleja is the hottest, driest corner of Portugal. Nights cool the plain a little; altitude cools Portalegre a great deal, and the Serra de São Mamede brings it rain the plain never sees.
terroir.soils: A patchwork, poor and shallow almost everywhere: granite around Portalegre, Évora and Reguengos, schist across much of the south around Vidigueira and Moura, and the marble belt of Estremoz, Borba and Vila Viçosa with clay and limestone around it. In the south the heat matters more than the rock.
terroir.topography: Mostly a gently rolling peneplain between two and four hundred metres, broken by low ridges, the Serra d'Ossa behind Redondo and the Serra do Mendro, the fault scarp at Vidigueira that divides the upper Alentejo from the lower. The one true mountain is the Serra de São Mamede on the Spanish border, where Portalegre's vineyards climb to seven hundred metres and more.
terroir.water: The Guadiana runs south through the east of the region and feeds the Alqueva reservoir, filled from 2002 and among the largest artificial lakes in western Europe, which irrigates the vineyards of the dry south-east. Elsewhere the small rivers run dry in summer and irrigation draws on dams and wells.

grapes.name: Aragonez
grapes.styles: Tempranillo under its southern name: ripe red fruit and soft tannin, early ripening, the backbone of most Alentejo blends and a mainstay of the vineyard.

grapes.name: Trincadeira
grapes.styles: Spice, pepper and freshness when it ripens cleanly on the dry plain, where it is safer from the rot that plagues it elsewhere; Tinta Amarela in the north.

grapes.name: Alicante Bouschet
grapes.styles: The French teinturier bred in 1866, red of flesh and juice, that found its best home here: colour, tannin, dark fruit and longevity, the grape of the traditional estates.

grapes.name: Castelão
grapes.styles: Freshness and raspberry fruit in the sandier south, less important here than on the Setúbal sand.

grapes.name: Touriga Nacional
grapes.styles: Planted since the 1990s for perfume and structure in the ambitious reds, often with Syrah.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: The international red that suits the heat best, ripe and peppery, in both the regional blends and single-varietal bottlings.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: A blending partner in the regional reds, ripening fully and easily on the plain.

grapes.name: Antão Vaz
grapes.styles: The Alentejo's own white, at home in Vidigueira: drought-tolerant, full, ripe tropical fruit and low acidity, so it is nearly always blended with Arinto and takes well to barrel.

grapes.name: Arinto
grapes.styles: The acid that survives the heat, blended with Antão Vaz and Roupeiro in almost every white.

grapes.name: Roupeiro
grapes.styles: An aromatic, early-drinking white, called Síria in the Beira Interior and Códega in the Douro, a traditional part of the white blend.

wines.note: A blend of Aragonez, Trincadeira and Alicante Bouschet, often with Syrah or Touriga: full, ripe, soft tannin, plum and dark cherry, a warm finish, a year in oak in the Reserva. The Alentejo's bread and butter, poured with grilled pork, lamb stew and the region's bread-and-garlic cooking.
The same grapes with the international ones from anywhere in the province, ripe and easy; much of the Alentejo's export volume carries this label.

Antão Vaz with Arinto and Roupeiro, sometimes Verdelho or Viognier: full, ripe, peach and citrus, best cold and young, some barrel-fermented for weight. It takes the region's fish soups and pork with clams.

Red, white or sometimes skin-contact white fermented and kept in clay talhas with the skins until Saint Martin's Day: rustic, textured, earthy and fresh, drawn from a tap at the base of the vessel. Serve cool with the cured meats and cheeses of the villages that make it.
From the granite slopes of the Serra de São Mamede, often old mixed vineyards: fresher, firmer and more fragrant than the plain's reds, picked weeks later, the Alentejo's claim to elegance.

made.viticulture: The Alentejo was a country of wheat, cork and sheep, and the vine was planted in earnest only from the 1980s, when the co-operatives were modernised and new estates were laid out on the plain in rows on wire, wide enough for machines, with drip irrigation from the start because a summer without rain allows nothing else. Irrigation is the region's defining choice: it keeps the vine alive and the yield steady, and the Alqueva reservoir has brought water to the hottest ground around Moura and Granja-Amareleja. Heat is the hazard, not rot; the canopy is managed for shade, picking begins in early August for the whites and runs through September, often at night to bring the fruit in cold, and the growers watch for sugar racing ahead of flavour and for acidity falling away. Portalegre is the exception that proves the rule: old bush vines on granite at six and seven hundred metres, mixed plantings of a dozen grapes picked together, rain from the mountain, a harvest weeks later than the plain and wines of real freshness. Cork oak stands in and around the vineyards everywhere; the montado is protected by law, the bark is stripped by hand once every nine years at the least, and the Alentejo is the heart of the world's cork production.
made.winemaking: The modern Alentejo red is made cleanly and ripely: destemmed, fermented in temperature-controlled stainless steel with pumping over, blended across grapes, aged in French and American oak barrels for the Reserva tier, bottled soft, and sold young. Alicante Bouschet brings the colour and tannin, Aragonez the flesh, Trincadeira the spice, Syrah the sweetness of fruit; the traditional estates still tread in stone lagares and age in large old wood for a longer-lived, tannic style. Whites are cold fermented and bottled early, with Antão Vaz sometimes fermented in barrel on its lees. Beside this stands a winemaking the Romans knew: the talha, a clay vessel of up to two thousand litres lined with pitch, in which destemmed grapes ferment with their skins, the cap punched down with a stick, the wine clarifying as the skins sink and settling under a seal of olive oil until it is opened on Saint Martin's Day, 11 November, and drawn from a tap at the base. The rules for Vinho de Talha DOC Alentejo, written into the appellation early in the 2010s, require the grapes to come from the sub-regions, the fermentation and the time on skins to pass in the talha, and the wine to stay there until that date. Vidigueira, with Vila de Frades, is the heartland, and a few co-operatives and many small cellars keep it.

law.classification: DOC Alentejo, run by the Comissão Vitivinícola Regional Alentejana at Évora, is not one block but eight separate demarcated sub-regions scattered across the province: Portalegre, Borba, Redondo, Évora, Reguengos, Granja-Amareleja, Vidigueira and Moura. A wine may be labelled Alentejo DOC alone or with the sub-region's name, and it must come from the sub-region's land and recommended grapes. The DOC's grape list is its own and not a native one: a core group that must make at least three quarters of a blend, Aragonez, Trincadeira, Alicante Bouschet and Touriga Nacional with Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon beside them, under the ordinance of 2010 and its annex of 2014. Everything between the sub-regions, which is most of the Alentejo, is Vinho Regional Alentejano, the IGP, with a longer grape list, widened again in 2018, and looser rules; a great deal of the region's best wine carries it by choice. Vinho de Talha is a category within the DOC with its own rules on vessel, skins and date. Reserva and Garrafeira follow the national definitions. The old distinction between Alto and Baixo Alentejo, upper and lower, is geography and not law.
tiers: DOC Alentejo
Wine from one of the eight demarcated sub-regions, with the DOC's core grapes (Syrah and Cabernet among them) at three quarters of the blend at the least; the sub-region's name may be added.
DOC Alentejo with a sub-region
Portalegre, Borba, Redondo, Évora, Reguengos, Granja-Amareleja, Vidigueira or Moura on the label: the whole wine from that sub-region.
Vinho de Talha DOC Alentejo
Wine fermented in clay talhas with its skins and held there until 11 November, from the DOC's grapes and land.
Vinho Regional Alentejano
The regional wine of the whole province, between and beyond the sub-regions, with a longer grape list and looser rules; much of the Alentejo's finest wine chooses it.
Vinho
Wine with no origin claim.
labels: Alentejo
The DOC: from one of the eight sub-regions.
Alentejano
The regional wine: from anywhere in the province.
Talha
The clay fermentation vessel; Vinho de Talha is the category.
Herdade, Monte
The Alentejo's words for an estate and for the farmhouse on it; the quintas of the north are herdades here.
Reserva
A vintage-dated wine with at least half a degree more alcohol than the regional minimum, usually oaked.

places.name: Portalegre
places.note: The northernmost sub-region, on the granite of the Serra de São Mamede against the Spanish border, with vineyards at six to seven hundred metres and higher: cooler, wetter, picked weeks after the plain, with old mixed bush vines that give the Alentejo's freshest and most fragrant reds and whites. The exam's Alentejo exception.

places.name: Borba
places.note: The marble country north-east of Évora with Estremoz and Vila Viçosa, on clay and limestone with marble outcrops: firm, balanced reds from Aragonez and Trincadeira, and a co-operative founded in 1955 whose cork-labelled red is a national standard.

places.name: Estremoz
places.note: The marble town beside Borba, on the sub-region's northern edge, home to some of the plain's most serious family estates.

places.name: Redondo
places.note: South of Borba under the Serra d'Ossa, on schist and granite: ripe, generous reds, a strong co-operative and a tradition of clay talhas in the village cellars.

places.name: Évora
places.note: The sub-region around the Roman and university city at the centre of the province, on granite and clay: the site of the Cartuxa cellar, named for the Carthusian monastery beside it, and of the icon red named after a medieval wine of the city, Pêra-Manca.

places.name: Reguengos
places.note: Reguengos de Monsaraz, east of Évora towards the Alqueva lake and the fortified hill village of Monsaraz, on granite, schist and clay: the home of the estate that led the Alentejo's modern revival in the 1980s, and of a big co-operative.

places.name: Granja-Amareleja
places.note: The south-eastern sub-region near Moura, the hottest and driest ground in Portugal, on schist: concentrated, low-yield reds from old bush vines, now irrigated from the Alqueva.

places.name: Vidigueira
places.note: Below the Serra do Mendro fault, where the plain drops into the lower Alentejo: the warmest and earliest of the sub-regions but for the south-east, the home of Antão Vaz for whites, and with Vila de Frades the heartland of talha wine.

places.name: Vila de Frades
places.note: The village of the talhas, where clay vessels stand in the cellars and the wine is opened on Saint Martin's Day; the capital of Vinho de Talha.

places.name: Moura
places.note: The southernmost sub-region, on the Guadiana near the Alqueva dam, hot and dry on schist and limestone: full, ripe reds from Aragonez, Trincadeira and Alicante Bouschet.

places.name: Alqueva
places.note: The reservoir on the Guadiana, filled from 2002 and one of the largest artificial lakes in western Europe, which brought irrigation to the dry south-east and water to Reguengos, Moura and Granja-Amareleja.

producers.name: Herdade do Mouchão
producers.why: The traditional Alentejo in one estate: Alicante Bouschet planted since the nineteenth century, trodden in stone lagares, aged in old wood, made to last decades.

producers.name: Herdade do Esporão
producers.why: The Reguengos estate whose winery of the 1980s led the Alentejo's modern revival and whose Reserva is one of the region's most widely known reds.

producers.name: Cartuxa, Fundação Eugénio de Almeida
producers.why: The Évora foundation that makes wine in a former Jesuit house beside the Carthusian monastery that named it, and bottles Pêra-Manca, the Alentejo's icon red, only in the years it judges fit.

producers.name: Adega de Borba
producers.why: The co-operative of the marble country, founded in 1955, whose cork-labelled Reserva taught a generation of Portuguese what an Alentejo red tastes like.

producers.name: Cortes de Cima
producers.why: A Vidigueira estate founded in 1988 that planted Syrah in the early 1990s, before the region's lists admitted it, and sold the wine unnamed as Incógnito; Syrah is on the Alentejo's lists now.

producers.name: Tapada do Chaves
producers.why: A Portalegre estate founded in 1901 with old mixed vineyards on the granite of São Mamede, the classic example of the mountain Alentejo.

producers.name: Adega Cooperativa de Vidigueira
producers.why: The co-operative of the talha heartland, which still ferments part of its wine in clay and is the easiest Vinho de Talha to find.

exam: Place the Alentejo as the broad inland south, a third of Portugal, hot and dry, and name the eight DOC sub-regions with Portalegre as the cool granite exception at altitude.
Give the red blend: Aragonez (Tempranillo), Trincadeira, Alicante Bouschet and Castelão, with Syrah and Touriga Nacional beside them.
Give the whites: Antão Vaz for body, Arinto for acidity, Roupeiro for aroma.
Know Alicante Bouschet as a French teinturier, red of flesh, that found its home here.
Define the talha and Vinho de Talha: clay vessel, skins in, opened on Saint Martin's Day, 11 November.
Separate Alentejo DOC (the eight sub-regions) from Vinho Regional Alentejano (the whole province).
Know the cork: the Alentejo's montado of cork oak, stripped every nine years at the least, supplies a large share of the world's wine corks.
traps: Aragonez is Tempranillo, the same grape as the Douro's Tinta Roriz; the Alentejo uses the southern name.
Alentejo on a label is the DOC from one of eight sub-regions; Alentejano is the regional wine from anywhere in the province.
Alicante Bouschet is a French crossing, not a Portuguese native, and one of the few red grapes with red juice.
Portalegre is not hot plain: it is granite at altitude in the Serra de São Mamede, picked weeks later, the freshest wine of the region.
A talha is a clay fermentation vessel, not a barrel; a lagar is the stone treading trough the traditional estates use.
Antão Vaz is the Alentejo's white; Arinto is blended in for acidity, Encruzado belongs to the Dão and Alvarinho to Vinho Verde.
Reguengos is Reguengos de Monsaraz; Monsaraz is the hill village, not a sub-region of its own.

cards.b: Portalegre, Borba, Redondo, Évora, Reguengos, Granja-Amareleja, Vidigueira and Moura.

cards.f: Alentejo DOC against Vinho Regional Alentejano
cards.b: DOC: from one of the eight sub-regions, on the DOC's own grape list. Alentejano: the whole province, a longer list and looser rules; much fine wine chooses it.
Aragonez (Tempranillo), Trincadeira and Alicante Bouschet, often with Castelão, Syrah or Touriga Nacional: ripe, soft, generous.
A French teinturier crossing of 1866, red flesh and red juice, that found its best home on the Alentejo plain: colour, tannin, long life.
Antão Vaz for ripe body (Vidigueira's grape), Arinto for acidity, Roupeiro for aroma; some Verdelho and Viognier.
A clay vessel of up to two thousand litres, lined with pitch, in which grapes ferment and rest with their skins under olive oil; opened on Saint Martin's Day, 11 November.

cards.f: The cool exception of the Alentejo
cards.b: Portalegre: granite in the Serra de São Mamede at six to seven hundred metres, rain from the mountain, old mixed vines, picked weeks after the plain.
The montado of cork oak, protected by law, stripped by hand at least nine years apart; the Alentejo is the heart of the world's cork supply.
One grape, Tempranillo: Aragonez in the Alentejo and the south, Tinta Roriz in the Douro and the Dão.

questions.q: Which sub-region of DOC Alentejo lies on granite at altitude in the Serra de São Mamede?
questions.exp: Portalegre sits against the Spanish border at six to seven hundred metres, with rain from the mountain and old mixed vines picked weeks after the plain. Vidigueira and Moura are among the warmest sub-regions and Reguengos is the big central one.

questions.q: Under which name does the Alentejo grow Tempranillo?
questions.exp: Aragonez is Tempranillo's southern Portuguese name and the backbone of the Alentejo's red blends; the same grape is Tinta Roriz in the Douro and the Dão.

questions.q: Which red grape of the Alentejo has red flesh and red juice?
questions.exp: Alicante Bouschet is a teinturier, a French crossing of 1866 whose pulp is coloured, and it gives Alentejo blends their depth and tannin; Trincadeira, Touriga Nacional and Tinta Caiada all have clear juice like almost every other red grape.

questions.q: In which vessel is Vinho de Talha fermented?
questions.exp: The talha is a large clay vessel lined with pitch in which the grapes ferment with their skins and rest under olive oil until Saint Martin's Day; the stone lagar is for treading, and casks and concrete belong to the modern cellar.

questions.q: On which date is the talha traditionally opened and the new wine first drawn?
questions.exp: Saint Martin's Day, 11 November, is the feast on which the talhas are opened across the Alentejo, and the Vinho de Talha rules require the wine to stay in the vessel with its skins until then.

questions.q: Which white grape gives Alentejo whites their body and is nearly always blended with Arinto for acidity?
questions.exp: Antão Vaz, at home in Vidigueira, is drought-tolerant and ripens to full tropical fruit with little acid, so Arinto is blended in. Encruzado is the Dão's white, Loureiro Vinho Verde's and Fernão Pires the Tejo's and Lisboa's.

questions.q: How many demarcated sub-regions make up DOC Alentejo?
questions.exp: Eight: Portalegre, Borba, Redondo, Évora, Reguengos, Granja-Amareleja, Vidigueira and Moura; the land between them is Vinho Regional Alentejano. The Tejo has six sub-regions and Vinho Verde nine.

questions.q: A label reads Vinho Regional Alentejano rather than Alentejo DOC. What does that tell you about the wine's origin?
opts: It may come from anywhere in the province
It comes from one of the eight demarcated sub-regions
It was fermented in a clay talha until Saint Martin's Day
It was grown on the granite of Portalegre at altitude
questions.exp: Alentejano is the IGP for the whole province, with a longer grape list and looser rules, and many of the region's best estates choose it; Alentejo DOC is reserved for wine from the eight demarcated sub-regions.

regions.name: Madeira
regions.summary: Madeira is a volcanic island in the Atlantic, nearer Morocco than Lisbon, and its wine is the one great wine made by heat on purpose. It is fortified, then either warmed in tanks for months, estufagem, or left in cask in warm lofts for years, canteiro, so that it arrives already oxidised and almost indestructible: an opened bottle keeps for months. Four noble white grapes run dry to sweet, Sercial, Verdelho, Boal and Malvasia, with Terrantez the rarity, and the red Tinta Negra makes most of the wine. Age statements run from three years to over fifty; Colheita is one harvest after five years in cask, Frasqueira one harvest and a single grape after twenty.

terroir.climate: Subtropical and maritime, warm all year with little frost, humid, and wet on the north coast where the trade winds drop their rain; the south coast around Funchal is drier and sunnier. Heat and humidity bring mildew and rot, so the vines are lifted off the ground and the grapes are picked early and acid. The climate that makes the vineyard difficult is the same one that ages the wine in the lofts.
terroir.soils: Volcanic: red and brown clay weathered from basalt, rich in iron and potassium, acid, held on the slopes by dry-stone walls. It is fertile enough to need no feeding and drains well, but there is little depth of it, and on Porto Santo the soil is sand and limestone instead.
terroir.topography: A steep island rising to Pico Ruivo at 1,862 metres within a few kilometres of the sea, so that almost every vineyard is a terrace, a poio, cut into a hillside or a cliff. Vines grow from sea level to about eight hundred metres, the noble grapes higher and cooler, Tinta Negra lower and on the north coast's wetter ledges.
terroir.water: The Atlantic on every side, moderating the heat and bringing the humidity; the levadas, the stone irrigation channels that carry water from the wet north across the mountains to the dry south, are what made the terraces farmable. Casks once crossed that ocean to the Indies and came home better, and the lodges learned to copy the voyage with heat.

grapes.name: Tinta Negra
grapes.styles: The red grape that makes most of Madeira, hardy and high yielding, vinified at every sweetness level for the three and five year blends and, since 2015, allowed to carry its name on the label; the best lodges show it can be serious.

grapes.name: Sercial
grapes.styles: The dry end of the noble ladder, grown highest and coolest: searing acidity, almond, dried lemon and salt, austere young and long-lived. It is Esgana Cão, dog strangler, on the mainland.

grapes.name: Verdelho
grapes.styles: Medium dry, from the cooler north coast: smoky, nutty, orange peel and a firm acid line, the classic aperitif and soup wine and the grape behind Rainwater's style.

grapes.name: Boal
grapes.styles: Bual in English: medium sweet, from the warm south coast, caramel, raisin, toffee and dried fig with the acidity still cutting; the cheese and dessert wine.

grapes.name: Malvasia
grapes.styles: Malmsey, the sweetest noble style, grown low on the warm south coast: dark toffee, coffee, candied orange and a long tangy finish; Malvasia de São Jorge is the usual planting now, Malvasia Cândida the original.

grapes.name: Terrantez
grapes.styles: A near-extinct noble grape between Verdelho and Boal in sweetness, fragrant and bitter-edged, bottled by only a few lodges and named by examiners for that reason.

grapes.name: Bastardo
grapes.styles: A rare red grape, Trousseau of the Jura, once common and now bottled as a curiosity in medium styles.

wines.note: Pale amber, dry, piercing acidity, almonds and dried citrus; serve cool as an aperitif with olives, salted almonds, consommé or smoked fish. The blind-tasting shock: fortified and bone dry.
Medium dry, golden, smoky and nutty with orange peel; cool, with soups, pâté, mushroom dishes and hard cheese.
Medium sweet, amber to brown, toffee and raisin with a tang of acid; cellar cool with cheese, caramel desserts, nut tarts and bread pudding.
Sweet and dark, coffee, dark toffee and candied orange, cut by acidity so it never cloys; with chocolate, pecan pie, blue cheese or alone after dinner.
A light, pale, medium-dry blend, usually Tinta Negra, named for the casks said to have been diluted by rain on the quay; the American market's Madeira, served cool as an aperitif or in cooking.

One harvest, a single grape, nearly always one of the nobles, at least twenty years in cask by canteiro before bottling: the summit of the island, intense, layered and apparently immortal, poured in small measures.

made.viticulture: Madeira's vineyards are terraces, poios, held by dry-stone walls on slopes that are often too steep for anything but a hoe, and they are tiny: the island is a place of smallholders who sell to the lodges, and a vineyard is a few rows beside a house, bananas and vegetables. The vine is trained on low pergolas, latadas, that lift the fruit into the breeze above the humidity, with the ground beneath sometimes cropped; wire training on the few flatter sites is recent. Rain, mildew and rot are the hazards, far more than drought, and the growers spray and pick early: the island wants acidity, not sugar, since the fortification will set the sweetness, and the grapes come in at modest ripeness through August and September, the lower warm south coast first and the high Sercial plots last. The noble grapes are a small minority of the plantings and are grown where they do best, Sercial and Verdelho high and on the north coast, Boal and Malvasia low on the sunny south coast around Câmara de Lobos and Calheta; Tinta Negra is everywhere. Oidium in 1852 and phylloxera in 1872 wrecked the old vineyard and brought in hybrid direct producers, which may not go into Madeira wine, and the replanting that followed is why Tinta Negra dominates. Porto Santo, the sandy sister island, grows a little on its own ground.
made.winemaking: The must ferments, with or without skins, and is fortified with neutral grape spirit to seventeen to eighteen per cent; a sweet style is stopped early with most of its sugar unfermented, a dry one is allowed to ferment almost out first, so the grape and the moment of fortification set the sweetness together. Estufagem warms the wine in tanks at around forty-five to fifty degrees for at least three months: the method for the three-year and most five-year blends, mostly Tinta Negra, invented in the 1790s to copy the sea voyage, the vinho da roda, that had improved casks sent as ballast to the Indies. Canteiro ages the wine in old casks on racks under the lodge roof, where the sun warms it slowly over years: the method for the noble grapes, the age-stated blends from ten years upwards, Colheita and Frasqueira, and the wine loses volume to evaporation and gains concentration, rancio and tang. Both routes give a wine already oxidised and stable, so an open bottle lasts months and a sealed one a century. Blends are assembled for an age statement and approved by tasting; Colheita is one harvest bottled after five years in cask; Frasqueira is one harvest of a single grape, nearly always noble, after twenty years in cask; a solera, dated to the year it was laid down, is a refreshed blend whose date is not a vintage. A varietal label needs 85 per cent of the grape, and the regulator seals every bottle.

law.classification: Madeira is a DOC of fortified wine regulated by IVBAM, the Instituto do Vinho, do Bordado e do Artesanato da Madeira, which tastes, approves and seals every lot. The wine must be fortified to between seventeen and twenty-two per cent from grapes of the island's authorised list, and the categories are set by age, by harvest and by grape rather than by vineyard. The age ladder runs three years, five (Reserve), ten (Special Reserve), fifteen (Extra Reserve), twenty, thirty, forty, fifty and over fifty, each a blend approved as showing the character of that age. Colheita, also sold as Harvest, is a single harvest bottled after at least five years in cask; Frasqueira, also Garrafeira or Vintage, is a single harvest of one grape, nearly always noble, aged at least twenty years in cask by canteiro. A grape on the label means at least 85 per cent of it; since 2015 Tinta Negra may be named like the nobles. Sweetness words, from extra seco to doce, may be used instead of or beside the grape. Rainwater is a defined light medium-dry style. The still wines of the island are a separate DOP, Madeirense, with the regional wine Terras Madeirenses.

places.name: Funchal
places.note: The capital and port on the south coast where the lodges stand and the wine is aged, blended and shipped; the city's lofts are where canteiro happens, and the oldest stocks on the island lie in its cellars.

places.name: Câmara de Lobos
places.note: The fishing town west of Funchal and the heart of the south coast vineyard, warm and sunny: the home of Tinta Negra, Boal and Malvasia and of two of the island's producing houses, with the terraces of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos climbing behind it and, to the west under a cliff, the Fajã dos Padres with its old Malvasia Cândida vines, reached by cable car.

places.name: Estreito de Câmara de Lobos
places.note: The parish above the town, the island's most important vine parish, where the terraces rise through the warm belt of Tinta Negra into Boal and, higher, Sercial and Verdelho.

places.name: Jardim da Serra
places.note: The high parish above Estreito, cool and often in cloud, where Sercial grows at the top of its range.

places.name: Calheta
places.note: The sunny south-western coast beyond Câmara de Lobos, warm enough for Malvasia and Boal low by the sea, with terraces of Tinta Negra above them.

places.name: São Vicente and the north coast
places.note: Wetter, cloudier and cooler, facing the trade winds: the north-coast parishes of São Vicente, Seixal and Porto Moniz grow Verdelho and Sercial on narrow ledges above the sea, and much Tinta Negra on the lower slopes.

places.name: Porto Santo
places.note: The flat, sandy sister island to the north-east, dry and hot, with a little wine of its own on sand and limestone, traditionally from the white Caracol and Listrão; its grapes may go into Madeira.

producers.name: Blandy's
producers.why: Founded in 1811 and the best known of the British names of the Madeira Wine Company, with the reference Frasqueiras and the Funchal lodge where canteiro can be seen.

producers.name: Henriques and Henriques
producers.why: A Câmara de Lobos house of 1850 with vineyards of its own, a dry-leaning style built on Sercial and Verdelho, and a reliable Terrantez.

producers.name: Barbeito
producers.why: The house, founded in 1946, that stopped adding caramel and showed what single-cask and unblended Tinta Negra could be.

producers.name: Broadbent
producers.why: An importer's label rather than a lodge: single-cask Madeiras selected for the North American market across the grape ladder.

producers.name: Cossart Gordon
producers.why: Founded in 1745, the oldest shipping name on the island, a brand of the Madeira Wine Company since the 1950s, known for a drier house style.

producers.name: Justino's
producers.why: Founded in 1870 and one of the island's largest producers, from three-year blends to very old Frasqueiras.

producers.name: Pereira d'Oliveira
producers.why: A family house of 1850 in Funchal famous for selling Frasqueiras from the nineteenth century directly from its lodge.

producers.name: Madeira Wine Company
producers.why: The group formed from the Madeira Wine Association of 1913 that gathered Blandy's, Cossart Gordon, Leacock's and Miles, most of the historic British names.

exam: Say the noble ladder dry to sweet: Sercial, Verdelho, Boal (Bual), Malvasia (Malmsey), with Terrantez as the rarity.
Explain the two ageing routes: estufagem, heated tanks for months, for the young blends; canteiro, cask in a warm loft for years, for the fine wines.
Know Tinta Negra as the red grape that makes most Madeira and may be named on the label since 2015.
Hold the numbers: fortified to seventeen to twenty-two per cent, 85 per cent for a varietal label, Colheita after five years in cask, Frasqueira after twenty.
Give the age ladder: 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 50 and over 50 years, each a blend approved by tasting.
Know that sweetness is set by the moment of fortification, early for sweet, late for dry.
Serve it: Sercial and Verdelho cool as aperitifs, Boal and Malmsey with cheese and dessert, and an open bottle keeps for months.
traps: Boal and Bual are one grape; Malvasia and Malmsey are one grape and one style. The ladder runs Sercial, Verdelho, Boal, Malvasia, driest to sweetest.
Frasqueira and Colheita are both single-harvest Madeiras, but Frasqueira needs twenty years in cask and a single grape, nearly always a noble one; Colheita five years and any grape.
A solera date is the year the solera was laid down, never a vintage.
Rainwater is a style, light and medium dry, not a grape and not a region.
Tinta Negra is red, and most Madeira is made from it; the noble grapes are a small minority of the vineyard.
Estufagem is the fast route in a heated tank; canteiro is the slow route in cask under the roof. Both cook the wine on purpose, and neither is a solera.
Madeira wine is fortified; the island's table wines are a separate appellation, Madeirense.
Sercial is grown high and cool, Malvasia low and warm: the sweet grape takes the sunniest ground.

cards.b: Sercial, Verdelho, Boal (Bual), Malvasia (Malmsey); Terrantez is the rare fifth, medium in style.

cards.f: How is a sweet Madeira made sweet?
cards.b: By fortifying early, while most of the sugar is unfermented; a dry Sercial is fortified after the ferment has nearly finished. Spirit to seventeen to eighteen per cent.
Single harvest, a single grape, nearly always a noble one, at least twenty years in cask by canteiro before bottling; also called Garrafeira or Vintage Madeira.
A single harvest bottled after at least five years in cask, from any grape, Tinta Negra included; younger and cheaper than Frasqueira.

cards.f: The grape that makes most Madeira
cards.b: Tinta Negra, a red, hardy and high yielding, vinified at every sweetness level; it may be named on the label since 2015.

cards.f: Why does an open bottle of Madeira keep?
cards.b: The wine is already oxidised and heated by its making, so air and warmth can do little more; months open, decades sealed.
A light, pale, medium-dry style, usually Tinta Negra, named for casks said to have been rained on at the quay; the traditional American market's Madeira.

questions.q: Which of Madeira's noble grapes makes the driest style?
questions.exp: The ladder runs Sercial, Verdelho, Boal, Malvasia from driest to sweetest; Sercial is grown highest and coolest and is fortified late, after the ferment has nearly finished.

questions.q: What is the name of the slow ageing method in which Madeira rests in cask in a warm loft for years?
questions.exp: Canteiro is the rack the cask rests on under the lodge roof, where the sun warms the wine over years; it is the route for the noble grapes, Colheita and Frasqueira, while estufagem heats young blends in tanks for months.

questions.q: Which grape makes the greater part of Madeira's wine?
questions.exp: Tinta Negra, a red, hardy and high yielding, is the island's dominant grape and the base of most three and five year blends; the noble whites together are a small minority, and Terrantez is nearly extinct.

questions.q: How many years must a Frasqueira Madeira spend in cask before it may be bottled?
questions.exp: Frasqueira, the single-harvest, single-grape vintage category, needs at least twenty years in cask by canteiro; Colheita needs five, Special Reserve is a ten-year blend and three years is the youngest Madeira.

questions.q: Which English name appears on export labels for Madeira made from Malvasia?
questions.exp: Malmsey is the English corruption of Malvasia, the sweetest noble style; in the same way Bual is the export spelling of Boal.

questions.q: At what moment in the process is the sweetness of a Madeira decided?
opts: When spirit is added to stop the fermentation
When the wine is heated in the estufa
When the blend is assembled for its age statement
When the wine is bottled and sealed
questions.exp: Fortification stops the yeast, so an early addition leaves a sweet Malvasia and a late one a dry Sercial; heating, blending and bottling come later and change the flavour, not the sugar.

questions.q: Which body regulates Madeira wine, approving each lot by tasting and sealing the bottles?
questions.exp: IVBAM is the Madeira institute for wine, embroidery and handicraft; the IVDP governs Port and Douro, the IVV is the national vine and wine institute, and the CVRA is the Alentejo's regional commission.

questions.q: What does the year on a solera Madeira record?
opts: The year the solera was first laid down
The harvest of every wine in the bottle
The year the wine was heated
The year the lodge was founded
questions.exp: A solera is a blend refreshed over time, and its date is the year it began, not a vintage; only Colheita and Frasqueira carry a true harvest year.
